practice.title: Respect Others
agreedSteps: Practice prostration and respecting others over the next two weeks. Key in to people's sufferings and problems — view their struggles as important, more important than our own. Respect the unseen battles people are fighting every day.

When we have difficulty respecting someone, recognize that our self-cherishing is what prevents us from respecting them. Dissolve the 'inherently unrespectable person' we normally see — they don't exist.
View difficult people as our teachers. They are specifically training us for something — teaching us to have the courage to stand up to bad behavior when needed, while still respecting the person.
steps: Try making a mental prostration at any point in the day — on the train, lying down, wherever. It can be as simple as thinking: I prostrate to the Buddhas, with the goal of destroying self-cherishing or gaining humility.
Use our body to show respect in culturally appropriate ways. Think about how we can physically lower ourselves and raise others — even a slight bow of the head qualifies as a physical prostration.
practice.quote: To prostrate means to respect others. How much do I respect others, and what does it mean to really respect someone? Not just be with someone, not just be nice to someone, but to respect them.

commentary.title: What Problem Does Prostration Solve?
content: Just as with every practice we've looked at, the question to ask is: what is the problem that prostration will solve for us? There are several. We might have lots of non-virtue that needs purifying — prostration has great power to purify non-virtue. We might need positive meritorious energy — prostration accumulates that. We might have a false sense of pride — prostration develops humility. We might lack faith or respect for our spiritual guide — the prostration form plants seeds for that.

Whether prostration actually works depends solely on our mind. If we approach it with a pure motivation — wishing to overcome pride and keeping the qualities of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha uppermost in our mind — beneficial effects will definitely follow. A 'pure motivation' doesn't mean perfect focus. It just means some spiritual component — not treating it purely as a workout.

commentary.title: Three Types of Prostration
content: Shantideva mentions two types of prostration — verbal and physical — and other texts add a third: mental prostration, which is the attitude of respect and faith we extend toward worthy objects. In the most beneficial form of practice, all three are performed simultaneously.

For physical prostrations, there are two methods in common use: the half-length prostration (kneeling, touching hands and forehead to the ground) and the full-length prostration (whole outstretched body in contact with the ground). But it should be noted that merely holding our hands at our heart, or even bowing our head slightly, qualifies as a physical prostration. It's not necessary to touch the ground at all.

commentary.title: Hands at Heart Is a Completely Perfect Prostration
content: There comes a point in every single person's life — unless they die of a random accident — where holding their hands at their heart is the only way they can physically prostrate anymore. That point will come to all of us one day. Maybe we're there, maybe it's tomorrow, maybe it's in 50 years. But it's not deficient in any way. It's not lesser than. It's a completely perfect prostration. It's a completely qualified choice, and we never have to feel bad about it.

When we can't do the half-length or full-length prostration — like sitting in chairs at a big event — it's actually a privilege in some ways. It gives us the freedom to really do the mental prostrating part well. When we do prostrations, we try to imagine infinite bodies prostrating for infinite eons, which is quite a big thing to do with the mind. When all we need to do is hold our hands at our heart, we can let our imagination go wild.

commentary.title: The Four-Point Touch and What It Plants
content: According to a widely followed tradition, we begin by placing the palms of our hands together with the thumbs touching and tucked inside, symbolizing a wish-fulfilling jewel. We then touch our folded hands to four places on our body to plant seeds for various qualities of an enlightened being.

First, the top of our head — to attain a Buddha's ushnisha, the crown protuberance that results from paying respect to our spiritual guide. So if we don't have a lot of faith or respect for our spiritual guide, prostration starts creating the cause for that. Then the forehead — a sign of wisdom, solving our ignorance problem. Then the throat — power of speech. Then the heart — power of mind. If our motivation and faith are strong, these practices place powerful potentialities in our mindstream for a Buddha's transcendent body, speech, and mind.
The tradition is that the four-point touch goes with the half-length and full-length prostrations. When we're just holding our hands at our heart, we don't need to do that.

commentary.title: Humility as the Antidote to Pride
content: One of the key problems prostration solves is our false sense of pride. A friend said that when she does prostrations, because she has this issue with pride, she thinks to the Buddhas and to her spiritual guide, 'May I be like the rug underneath your feet.' Every time she prostrates. Which is offensive to our self-cherishing mind — but it's a beautiful, humble attitude. May I be the very rug beneath your feet. The self is nothing.

Naropa, Marpa's principal guru, used prostrations as his chief external method for accumulating merit. Je Tsongkhapa performed three and a half million full-length prostrations during a retreat — famously eroding a little ditch in the ground from his skin rubbing the rock. Jampa Rinpoche, said to be a manifestation of Maitreya Buddha, limited his external merit practices to just two things every day: offering one hundred water bowls and making one hundred prostrations. Even into old age he continued this practice.

commentary.title: Prostration Means Respecting Others
content: When Geshe-la has taught about prostration as a practical tool for daily life, he especially taught that to prostrate means to respect others. This is a big area of investigation. How much do I respect others, and what does it mean to really respect someone? Not just be with someone, not just be nice to someone, but to respect them. There's an elevation of that person when we respect them. It's not putting up with them — it's really respecting them.

Bowing our head slightly is showing a physical gesture of respect appropriate for the society we're in. As bodhisattvas — trainee bodhisattvas — we're always thinking: how can I fit in with society and other people's norms so that I can benefit them? We're not trying to impose our own moral judgments on them.

commentary.title: The Four Intervention Points
content: There are only a few intervention points where we can make things move in our mind. Think upstream, downstream. Downstream are the actual states of mind we develop — love, compassion, respect, and so on. We can't just make them happen out of nothing. They're downstream of only four things we can do: what we pay attention to, how we label things (discrimination), what our intention is, and what we're mindful of — what we're remembering.

It's like a waterfall. The compound minds — love, compassion, respect for others — are at the pool at the bottom. At the top there are just four little spouts: attention, discrimination, intention, and mindfulness. We have to turn on one of those spouts to get things moving. A lot of times we get into trouble because we're standing at the bottom of the pool going, 'Where's the love? Where's the compassion? Come on, go away, delusions!' When really we need to trot up to the top of the waterfall and work on those spouts.

Relabeling is working the discrimination spout. You can't just jump to cherishing others instantly — but you can start by labeling everyone 'friend.' Even if you don't mean it. Do it over and over, and the spout will completely open up and the water will flow.
commentary.quote: A lot of times we get into trouble because we're standing at the bottom of the pool going, where's the love? Where's the compassion? What we really need to do is trot up to the top of the waterfall and start working on some of those spouts.

commentary.title: Everything Is a Tantric Practice in Disguise
content: Basically everything is a tantric practice in disguise. That's how Geshe-la has taught the teachings — everything is from the point of view of Highest Yoga Tantra. Like equanimity: level one is friend, enemy, stranger — moving everyone into the friend bucket. Equanimity level seventeen or something is put everyone in the Vajrayogini bucket. It's one practice — equanimity. A tantric master teaches at the level of sutra so everyone can practice it, but it's seeding the realizations of tantra from day one.
We can start to see this depth in every single practice. And it's really actually quite delightful to discover these connections, because it makes us appreciate the ingenuity of the presentation.
